title: Speech at work
hook: right speech in meetings and messages
tomorrow: what does a boss owe you, and what do you owe back?

segments.voice: Yesterday: effort without strain. Tune the string, not tighter and not looser. Today the string is your voice.

A message that starts per my last email can be heard from across the office. Tone travels, even in text. A thumbs-up can read as fine, or as furious. So how do you put a hard thing kindly? A short sutta gives a five-part test for speech that's well spoken, and it fits on a sticky note. Spoken at the right time. True. Gentle. Helpful. And said with a mind of goodwill.
screen: `PER MY LAST EMAIL.` → `TONE TRAVELS.` → `TIMELY, TRUE, GENTLE, HELPFUL, KIND.`

segments.voice: In Pali, the word for it is subhasita: well spoken. Now notice how much of that list is sound, not content. Two of the five are about what you say: is it true, does it help. The other three are about how it lands: when, how gently, from what heart. A true thing said at the wrong moment, or barked, or sent to win, fails the test even if every word is accurate. Elsewhere the Buddha describes his own speech the same way. He says what is true and beneficial, even when it's unwelcome, but he knows the right time to say it. So a hard message at work isn't a choice between honest and kind. It's both, tuned. Say the true thing. Say it when the other person can take it in, not at eleven at night. Use the softest words that are still clear. Make sure it helps the work, not just your mood. Check the heart it comes from. And here's the part for the ears: read it out loud before you send it. Your ear catches what your eyes skip. The edge in as I already said. The chill in a one-word fine. If it sounds like a slammed door, it reads like one.
screen: `SUBHASITA: WELL SPOKEN.` · `TWO ARE WHAT; THREE ARE HOW.` · `TRUE, EVEN UNWELCOME, AT THE RIGHT TIME.` · `READ IT OUT LOUD FIRST.` · then, large: `KIND AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Think of one true, kind message you could send someone you work or study with: a thanks, a heads-up, a clear no. Type it, then read it aloud, quietly, and listen. Soften one word if it needs it, and send it if it's ready.
Speech at work: words that are timely, true, gentle, helpful and said with goodwill, even when the news is hard.
Your line: kind at work. True, and in a voice someone can take in. Four of fifty.

howItsDone: Right speech is a factor of the eightfold path, and Buddhist teachers offer the five factors of well-spoken speech as a check before speaking or writing.

fork.setup: a coworker's part of the project has mistakes, it's due tomorrow, and it's 11 p.m. what fits well-spoken speech?
options: message first thing tomorrow: what you found, gently, and how to fix it.
send it now while it's fresh, and blunt, so they can't miss it.
fix it yourself and say nothing, so nobody's feelings get hurt.
fork.reveal: true and helpful, at a time it can be heard, gently and with goodwill: all five. silence skips the truth; blunt at midnight skips the rest.

original.note: Pali: subhasita, well spoken; AN 5.198 names the five factors of speech that is well spoken.

trapdoor: what you thought: kind speech means sugarcoating.

chat.says: drafting a text to petrov: i won't call the frames museum quality. it sounds... kind of rude?
options: Read it aloud first. Keep it true, soften the tone, offer words you can use.
Skip the text. Kind speech means never raising anything uncomfortable.
Send it now, as is. If it's true, how it sounds doesn't really matter.
chat.meaning: Well-spoken speech is timely, true, gentle, helpful and said with goodwill. A hard message can pass all five if you tune how it lands.

tie.story: The Buddha said well-spoken words are timely, true, gentle, helpful and said with goodwill.
